newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: TransAlta NZ says not pursuing Wairarapa.
newsitem.headline: TransAlta NZ says not pursuing Wairarapa.

text.p: The Wellington arm of Canadian power company TransAlta was not pursuing Wairarapa Electricity as a takeover target "at this stage", it said late on Monday.
TransAlta was always on the lookout for investments, but "at this stage we are not pursuing Wairarapa Electricity", a company spokesman told the NZPA new agency.
Shares in Wairarapa's owner South Eastern Utilities gained a further six cents to close at NZ$1.20 on Monday.
The stock had risen 5 cents on Friday reflecting rumours, and media reports, of an independent valuation of the stock at $1.30 and an imminent takeover by Wellington-based TransAlta NZ.
South Eastern Utilities, responding to a price query from the Stock Exchange during Monday, said there were no "matters of importance" concerning it that it was about to announce to the exchange.
Analysts, while acknowledging that TransAlta was the best placed major player to extract value from Wairarapa, had mixed views on the likelihood of a deal proceeding and the price.
"This $1.20-$1.30, or whatever it is, is just fruitland," one analyst who declined to be named, said.
The network businesses of Wairarapa carry an ODV value, an industry standard valuation, of $62 million.
TransAlta's past acquisitions -- of Capital Power and former Hutt Valley business EnergyDirect -- were made at ODV multiples of 1.45 and 1.19 times respectively.
The analyst said that buying record, and the poor performance expected from Wairarapa's Haunui windfarm, meant any offer price from TransAlta would not be that high.
"They're not going to pay much for the windfarm. They won't pay a book value, so it's way lower than what we've got at the moment."
Wairarapa's $8 million investment in the 3.5MW windfarm has long been considered marginal by the industry.

The company last year estimated it had made an on-going $1.5 million after-tax gain from reduced transmission prices, but that was expected to have further reduced the relative price advantage of the farm's output.
The analyst said his understanding was that about a month ago, South Eastern had employed a broker to seek offers for Wairarapa.
"They blew the kiss to TransAlta," he said. "TransAlta looked, about a month ago, and didn't do anything."
South Eastern is 50.2 percent owned by Christchurch-based Pyne Gould Corporation and was formerly known as Amuri Corporation.
It took over Wairarapa Electricity last year and its only other major asset is a 28 percent stake in the Port of Timaru.

In January South Eastern Utilities reported a net profit for the December half of $2.51 million, down from the $6.25 million for the same period last year. The previous result was boosted by abnormal gains from asset sales of $5.45 million.
At the time the company reaffirmed forecasts for a June year after-tax profit of not less than $4.5 million, and not less than $5.7 million in 1998.
The analyst said that while Wairarapa was "terrible" as a growth story, South Eastern had done very well in generating cash from the business.
Chief executive George Gould, he said, had been the first in the industry to work out that as much money could be made from a rural power network as from an urban one.
The problem now was that, given how far ahead of the industry Wairarapa was in terms of charges, a new owner had little scope to make more money except by cutting out another head office structure.
If the reported valuation was correct and was based on free-cash flows, Wairarapa's earnings were probably "way above" the government's theoretical regulatory cap.
"I'd personally question whether the earnings it's got at the moment are sustainable," he said.
